cards.title: Fully polynomial randomized approximation of mixed discriminants
cards.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the mixed discriminant of every tuple of rational symmetric positive semidefinite matrices, with no restriction on dimension, rank or conditioning? The scheme must give arbitrarily small relative error with success probability at least \(3/4\), in the precise uniform bit model below.
cards.definitions:
The input contains an integer \(n\geq1\), exactly \(n\) symmetric matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), and a rational accuracy parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1\). A matrix \(A_i\) is positive semidefinite if \(z^{\mathsf T}A_i z\geq0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). All entries, including zeros, are given explicitly in row order. Integers are encoded in binary; a rational is a signed numerator and a positive denominator, also in binary with delimiters. Let \(L\) denote the full input length, including the dimensions, matrix entries and accuracy parameter. Symmetry and positive semidefiniteness are promises; malformed data can be rejected, and there is no approximation guarantee outside these promises.

With commuting formal variables \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), define
\[
D(A_1,\ldots,A_n)
=[t_1\cdots t_n]\det\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n t_iA_i\right).
\]
The notation \([t_1\cdots t_n]\) means the coefficient of that monomial in the determinant polynomial. Equivalently it is the mixed partial derivative with respect to all \(n\) variables, evaluated at zero. This is the unnormalized coefficient convention: \(D(I_n,\ldots,I_n)=n!\), where \(I_n\) is the identity matrix. The alternative convention dividing by \(n!\) describes the same approximation question after multiplying outputs by that known factor, but this card uses only the displayed convention.

For positive semidefinite inputs, \(D\) is a nonnegative rational number. To see nonnegativity, express each matrix as a sum of real rank-one matrices \(v v^{\mathsf T}\). Multilinearity expands \(D\) into nonnegative terms: for one vector from each matrix the term is \(\det[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n]^2\). This identity is a mathematical description, not an assumption that arbitrary real vectors or their exact decompositions are freely available to the algorithm.

A fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, abbreviated FPRAS, is one uniform randomized multitape Turing machine \(M\) for all promised tuples and all rational \(\varepsilon\) in the stated range. It always outputs a nonnegative rational \(Z\), encoded by binary numerator and positive denominator, and satisfies
\[
\Pr_{\rho}\left[(1-\varepsilon)D\leq M(A_1,\ldots,A_n,\varepsilon;\rho)\leq(1+\varepsilon)D\right]\geq\frac34.
\]
Its random bits \(\rho\) are independent and fair. There are fixed integers \(K,d\geq1\) bounding every computation by \(K(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence. Finite programs have no advice or oracle; random-bit generation, output length and all numerical precision are charged. The time requirement is worst case, not merely expected time. The exponent cannot depend on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\).

Singular and zero matrices are included. If \(D=0\), the success event requires \(Z=0\); as for every other input, it must hold with probability at least \(3/4\). On a positive input, an additive-error guarantee is insufficient when \(D\) is tiny. The promise imposes no positive lower bound on eigenvalues, no rank bound, no common eigenbasis, and no entrywise nonnegativity: a positive semidefinite matrix can have negative off-diagonal entries. The accuracy parameter is part of the input, so an algorithm for only a fixed constant relative error does not suffice. Independent repetition and a median can amplify the fixed success probability if desired, but amplification is not an additional target.

context_blocks.text: The diagonal case is the permanent. Given an entrywise nonnegative rational matrix \(B=(b_{ij})\), set \(A_i=\operatorname{diag}(b_{i1},\ldots,b_{in})\). Expanding the determinant gives \(D(A_1,\ldots,A_n)=\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_i b_{i,\sigma(i)}\), where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \([n]\). The known permanent FPRAS handles this subclass, while exact permanent hardness also establishes exact-computation hardness for the general mixed discriminant. Exact hardness alone does not preclude randomized relative approximation.

Another tractable special case is a tuple of rank-one matrices \(A_i=v_iv_i^{\mathsf T}\) with explicitly given rational vectors: the answer is one squared determinant. General positive semidefinite matrices are sums of rank-one terms, and expansion asks for the sum of squared determinants over all choices of one term from each matrix. The number of choices can be exponential, so the rank-one identity does not give the requested general algorithm.

Gurvits develops convex-relaxation methods giving multiplicative approximations whose factor can grow exponentially with dimension, and explicitly singles out the FPRAS question. A dimension-dependent exponential factor and a factor arbitrarily close to one are different guarantees even when both algorithms run in polynomial time.

A determinantal point process assigns a subset a weight given by a principal minor of a positive semidefinite kernel; its normalizing constant is the sum of those weights. Imposing partition or budget constraints changes which subsets contribute. The 2017 paper connects the resulting constrained sums to mixed discriminants, explaining why efficient unconstrained determinantal sampling does not automatically solve the constrained problem.

The 2017 reductions use rank-one decompositions and determinant identities. The coefficient convention is fixed explicitly here because factorial normalizations differ across presentations; known positive factors do not alter FPRAS existence when converted consistently. The real-vector identity explaining nonnegativity is separate from a claim that real arithmetic has unit cost in the rational-input benchmark.

Ohsaka and Matsuoka study products of determinantal point processes and relate the normalizing constant for two positive semidefinite kernels to mixed discriminants. Their hardness results for more general matrix classes or larger products do not themselves establish impossibility of an FPRAS for this positive-semidefinite mixed-discriminant target. The two-matrix connection illustrates the broader reach of the unresolved relative-approximation question.

cards.why: An FPRAS would extend the success of nonnegative permanent approximation to general positive semidefinite matrix tuples and improve the algorithmic understanding of constrained determinantal distributions. An impossibility result would identify a substantive boundary between determinant-based counting structures despite their nonnegative coefficients and useful convex relaxations.

progress.text: Gurvits explicitly asks whether an FPRAS exists for mixed volume or mixed discriminant, beyond dimension-dependent multiplicative approximations.
Celis and coauthors relate mixed discriminants to partition- and budget-constrained determinantal sums and record the missing general FPRAS.
Ohsaka and Matsuoka connect mixed discriminants to the normalizing constant for a product of two determinantal point processes.

cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an FPRAS exists, or a proof in Lean that no uniform randomized algorithm satisfies the specified approximation and worst-case time guarantees. A positive answer must cover all dimensions, all rational positive semidefinite tuples, every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the zero case, binary precision costs and the success probability. A negative answer must rule out the full class of schemes; failure of a particular estimator or Markov chain is insufficient.

This is a yes-or-no question about a relative-error approximation scheme, not a request for one additive approximation to a numerical constant. The benchmark’s absolute \(1/100\) convention for number-valued answers does not replace the requirement for all \(\varepsilon\). Exponentially coarse multiplicative estimates, fixed-rank or well-conditioned special cases, exact-computation hardness alone, and conditional impossibility under an unproved assumption do not settle the unconditional target.
cards.status_note: The 2007 source explicitly poses the FPRAS question; the checked 2017 and 2020 primary papers retain it and explain related constrained determinantal problems. A targeted later-work search on 16 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of this precise rational positive-semidefinite target. This dated, bounded review is not an exhaustive certification of current openness or an independent verification of every cited reduction.

sentences: The mixed discriminant is a fixed coefficient of a determinant polynomial built from positive semidefinite matrices.
The question asks for one randomized algorithm giving arbitrary relative accuracy in time polynomial in the input size and inverse accuracy.
The full rational-input model includes singular matrices, zero answers and badly conditioned matrices.
Permanents and single squared determinants are special cases, while constrained determinantal sums illustrate why the general case matters.
An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility of the full approximation scheme in Lean.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
